implementation_notes: Swift 5.5 moved the pattern into the language: an async function suspends instead of blocking, await collects the result and rethrows its error, async let starts two or more independent calls and awaits them together, and Task { } starts an unstructured unit of asynchronous work whose value/result is the handle. The compiler is part of the mechanism: actor isolation makes the hop back to the caller's state explicit, Sendable checking turns data races into compile errors, and structured concurrency (withTaskGroup, child tasks) guarantees that children are joined or cancelled with their parent, so the ownership rule the classic pattern had to document is enforced instead. Task.detached opts out of inherited context and priority, and unstructured Task drops errors unless its result is observed. Use it for all new Swift concurrency code, and bridge to the completion-handler variant only at APIs that have not adopted it.
pitfalls: An unstructured Task is not awaited by its parent: a thrown error is dropped unless value/result is observed - detached tasks inherit nothing at all (no priority, no task-locals, no cancellation).
Cancellation is cooperative and only a Bool: code must check Task.isCancelled or call try Task.checkCancellation() at suspension points, otherwise the work runs to completion.
Blocking a cooperative thread (semaphores, Thread.sleep, synchronous locks) inside async code can deadlock the shared pool; use Task.sleep and continuations instead.
Data shared with a task must be Sendable; wrapping non-Sendable mutable state compiles only through isolation or @unchecked Sendable, which silently reintroduces the race.
A task inherits the actor context, so an unstructured Task started from the main actor performs its synchronous prefix on the main actor until the first await.

variants.name: Completion handlers with @escaping closures
variants.implementation_notes: The pre-5.5 realization and the only interface of many existing APIs: the asynchronous method returns immediately and takes an @escaping closure that receives the result (or a Result<Success, Error>) when the work finishes, so the callback is the notification and the collection step simultaneously. It remains justified at the boundary of frameworks that have not adopted Swift concurrency - and the sanctioned bridge into async code is withCheckedContinuation, which wraps the handler and enforces the exactly-once resume rule that the raw style leaves to the programmer. Keep the handler style out of new code: it cannot express structured concurrency, spreads error handling across closure boundaries, and makes cancellation impossible to thread through.
pitfalls: The closure can be invoked twice or never; withCheckedContinuation turns exactly-once resumption into a runtime diagnostic, raw handlers do not.
Capturing self strongly in an escaping handler creates retain cycles and keeps view/controller state alive long after the call ended.
There is no cancellation channel: a handler-based call keeps running, so callers must ignore stale results by hand (a token or a generation counter).
Handlers may run on an arbitrary queue or the caller's queue depending on the API; UI updates must hop to @MainActor/the main queue and shared state must be synchronized.
